speechtext:
I table return to an order moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) for a copy of all orders in council passed since July 15,1943, which amend, suspend or otherwise alter the operations of statutes, and so on. The hon. member will remember asking me last year if the government would not consider having these amendments presented in a form which would make them readily available to members of the house. I am glad to be able to inform him that this has been done. I would inform my hon. friend and other hon. members that a consolidated table of contents and reference index published quarterly by the privy council office as an appendix to the weekly publication "Canadian War Orders and Regulations" contains these various amendments to statutes. This is a quarterly consolidation including specific reference to statutes amended, suspended or referred to by order in council. The latest consolidation covers the last quarter of 1943. The consolidation for the first quarter of 1944, up to March 31, 1944, will be published shortly.

1.	Respecting assistance to ex-members of the R.C.M.P., is there any fund, apart from pension or retirement, available for assistance to aged members of the force who are not on pension and have been rendered indigent?
2.	If so, what is this fund, and how is it administered?
3.	Is there any system of assistance in hospitalization for ex-members of the R.C.M.P.?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	No. None, except that established by section 21 of the R.C.M. Police Act, which is known as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police benefit trust fund, and which is composed of awards, portions of fines, seizures, etc., granted to serving members of the Force. From this fund, grants may be made, under the authority of the Minister of Justice, in accordance with regulations laid down by the governor in council in the following cases:
(a)	to any member of the force who, through disability, not due to his own fault, is discharged therefrom without being eligible for pension or gratuity, a sum not exceeding $200; or to any ex-member of the force who is in receipt of pension or compensation not exceeding $500 per annum and who, by reason of sickness or any cause not due to his own fault, is financially embarrassed, a sum not exceeding $200.
(b)	to any member of the force, who by reason of sickness or accident to a member of his family, or from any cause not due to his own fault, is financially embarrassed, a sum not exceeding $200, but any payment for this cause shall be made only when for the direct benefit of the family.
(c)	to any member of the force, in recognition of outstanding acumen, zeal or resourcefulness in bringing an important investigation to successful conclusion, a sum not exceeding $200.
(d)	to any member of the force, as recognition of any act of special endurance or bravery in the execution of duty, a sum not exceeding $200.
(e)	to any person designated by the minister, an amount not exceeding $75, to be applied on account of the burial expenses of any ex-member of the force who dies without leav-

Questions
ing sufficient means to provide for the cost of reasonable burial expenses, if no other source is available from which the necessary moneys may be obtained.
(f)	if a member of the force dies in the service and his widow and/or children may not be granted a pension or gratuity, if in need of financial assistance, there may be paid an amount not exceeding $300 in any one year to the widow, and to each child under fifteen years of age an amount not exceeding $60 in any one year.
(g)	for the purchase of recreation and mess equipment for the general benefit of any post or detachment, an amount not exceeding $3 per head in any year, the distribution to be based on the average strength of personnel for the post or detachment.
(h)	to members of the force generally, a lump sum annual payment, the amounts, basis of distribution and the date to be determined by the Minister in control of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
(i)	for the purpose of purchasing clothing, comforts, smoking material, or similar articles, for any members of the force on leave from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or who leave that force with the definite intention of proceeding on active service either in the naval, military or air forces of His Majesty, an amount not exceeding $3 per head, in any calendar year.
(j)	to any member of the force who sustains a loss or damage to personal effects or property in the performance of duty whilst attempting to make an arrest, or as the result of a motor-car accident, or any other cause or similar circumstance while on duty, and in which the Canadian government may either be unwilling or unable to reimburse him-an amount not exceeding $100.
(k)	to any member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who may be discharged from the force while still in hospital or who may be invalided from the force and who may still require medical and hospital treatment, if he is unmarried, a grant not exceeding $150 in any one year but if he is married, an amount not exceeding $500 in any one year and to each child under fifteen years of age an amount not exceeding $60 in any one year, irrespective of the fact that the member of the force concerned may be eligible for a pension.
Each case in which a grant is recommended is investigated by the force and is dealt with according to its merits and within the limits of the regulations set by order in council.
As the Royal Canadian Mounetd Police benefit trust fund only began in 1921, it is not yet twenty-three years old, and it is
obvious that any ex-member of the force who left it more than twenty-three years ago did not make any contribution, either directly or indirectly, to the fund.

I have had several letters and many complaints with respect to the question of mail for overseas. Many examples have come to my notice, one in particular respecting a mother who has two boys in Italy. One of those boys received the odd letter, but he has not received one parcel since last July. The other boy has received neither letter nor parcel for months, and she writes them once or twice a week, as well as sending them parcels. Another woman Whose husband is overseas writes him quite often, but he has had only four letters in the last four or five months from her. Another mother sent parcels overseas for Christmas. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say just a word about these estimates. In the first place the committee understands that these estimates are for the present fiscal year which ends on March 31-that is to-morrow. They are in the nature of the additional amounts required to pay some of the expenditures of the present fiscal year. They do not touch matters relating to the next fiscal year. It is on matters that relate to the next fiscal year that the main estimates have been prepared, and it is on the main estimates that questions of government policy and the like are appropriately discussed. Hon. members know that in dealing with estimates the rule is that discussion must be confined to the item before the committee, but on the main estimates there is not infrequently an understanding that a general discussion shall be permitted on one of the items. That rule does not apply to individual items in supplementary estimates dealing with the present fiscal year.
I have no objections to hon. members, if they so desire, seeking to have it appear that ministers may not be wholly prepared to answer every question asked at this time. The ministers have taken into consideration the character of the estimates, namely that they are simply supplementary amounts required to make good small amounts needed to square accounts. The details given in the statement before us are in themselves pretty nearly enough to explain the items, which for the most part are for the payment of bonuses, for temporary assistance and things of the kind. Clearly it would be quite wrong to expect a discussion of general policy relating to agriculture or other subjects under items of this kind.
May I say to my hon. friend in regard to agriculture that there has been more time taken up in the house with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the coming year than with respect to any other department. The minister has devoted three, four . or five sittings to discussions of agricultural estimates. As I recall it, he had two sittings before he could get a single item through, and hon. gentlemen were at that time questioning him with regard to matters of general policy. I submit that the time of this house is precious at the moment and it is not in order to expect
the ministry to go beyond the items that appear on this particular paper in giving such explanations as can be given.

Is the

speechtext: May I draw the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that in the February number of "Canada at War" it is stated that, I believe, twenty-five such families had left for Canada on January 25. One of my reasons for asking the question I did was to endeavour to find out whether any actually have come or are in process of coming, because nothing seems to have developed from the visit of the immigration official to Lisbon.
Is my hon. friend speaking of movements from Portugal and Spain?
Yes.

hundred, including family members-have left, and I was under the impression that they are here now. I can ascertain whether that is so.

I wish the minister would clear it up, because, as I say, I was in touch with his department within the last two weeks, and the statement in "Canada at War" was definitely contradicted. The further statement was made that it was not improbable that a few family units would start to move from there during the month of March.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion on this item, but I suggest to the Prime Minister that as soon as we possibly can, after Easter, a day should be set aside for the discussion in this house of matters relating to the Department of External Affairs. An item in the estimates for the Department of External Affairs has already been called, so that the department is in; on that occasion, while some of us would have liked to ask questions regarding Canada's external relationships, we refrained from doing so because we realized that the government wanted to get that department into supply. But last year it was pretty well toward the end of the session before we were able to discuss the many matters in which hon. members ought to be interested, and in which many of them are interested, dealing with our external relationships.
This is only, of course, one phase. I think personally that we have done very badly by the refugee. I think that when the story of this part of our war assistance is written it will be a pretty sorry story so far as Canada is concerned. But at the moment I am speaking more particularly of the international situation, and the fact that Canada has played an important part in this war. I have followed with a good deal of misgiving the recent developments in the international field. International relationships, among the great powers particularly, have deteriorated in the past three or four months, and it is time that some of the smaller nations-if you will- gave much more attention- to external affairs than they have been giving to that subject. I notice that the Prime Minister of Great Britain said two weeks ago that the principal powers would have to do something. It is not good enough to leave these matters in the hands of the so-called principal powers. This house should seriously consider and discuss Canada's position in relation- to external affairs, giving full support to every measure and every necessary step for the winning of the war, yet considering also the problems which are arising and will arise. I ask the
Prime Minister that as early as possible after the recess we have a day to discuss external affairs, so that it may not be left until near the end of the session.

After that lecture to the government and to the principal powers, I desire to ask the Prime Minister a concrete question. What is the status of these refugees who are coming or have arrived, whichever it may be? Are they to be temporary guests of Canada, or are they to take up their domicile here permanently?

I might say in response to the previous question asked, that I telephoned the director of immigration and am informed that a party of refugees from Spain and Portugal, to the number of two hundred and fifty-six, is on its way and is expected in North America within a few days.
With regard to the question just asked by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the situation is this. These refugees for the time being are being given an asylum in- Canada; that is, they can remain here until the war is over and later on their status if they then desire to remain here, can be considered and determined. For the moment they are coming in simply as refugees; that is they are getting asylum in Canada for the duration of the war.
They are temporary guests.
Are any members of the party which the minister has mentioned going to the United States, or are they all coming to Canada?
I am speaking only of those who are coming to Canada. What the United States may be doing in the matter I am not in a position at the moment to say.

This is the forty-first day of the session, and this item is the first regarding external affairs which has appeared. True, the particular item is a five or six thousand dollar vote for an intergovernmental committee regarding refugees; but one of the most important subjects we have to consider is the whole question of external affairs, our relation to foreign policy, to empire policy, to refugees and the other subjects with which the department deals. There was a good deal of immigration from Continental Europe before the war and people are asking questions that should be answered. I moved for a return this session and it was brought down, and I think that the minister should make a statement not only about refugees but on the broader question about what is going to be
Supply-External Affairs

done first regarding immigration from the British isles, where people have suffered from the war more than they have anywhere else, and regarding migration within the empire.
The same practice is being followed this session as was followed at the last session, . because then it was only on the 114th day of the session that external affairs were discussed. I have every respect for the Prime Minister and I know that he is carrying a heavy load, but I suggest that shortly after the Easter recess there should be a day or two devoted to this very important topic, which we have been ignoring right along. The question of refugees comes under the department.
The other day we had a statement before the Empire club by a Mr. Kirkconnell, who in 1942 was engaged by the Minister of National War Services to write a book on continental and other immigration. He told the Toronto Empire club last week that there was no room in Canada for these refugees, but I do not pay a great deal of attention to that because he said the same thing on January 14, 1942, in Convocation hall. He said there was no room for any more British born in this country-and I may say that his book was widely distributed in England after the battle of Dunkirk.
The people should know the facts; they should know what is going on in this important department of immigration. I do not object to this item; in fact, I would like to see all these supplementary items pass as quickly as possible. But with all due respect to the cabinet, and admitting the work they have to do, I suggest that they might have set aside one or two days for external affairs, which is one of the most important matters before us. All others are subsidiary to it, and the refugee question is coordinated with it. I hope that the government will see fit to 'set aside a specified time for the discussion of these external affairs matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In reply to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) and to my hon. friend, who evidently did not hear his remarks, which were the same as his own-
Not quite the same.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-may I say that I am as anxious as anyone to oblige hon. members, but I would point out that it is not possible to oblige everyone and at the same time have a programme which it would be possible to carry out.
With reference to external affairs, the main policy of the government is to win the war, and the first step in that direction is to have

supplies voted by this house for war needs. The war appropriation measure was among the first brought before the house this session and it has not yet been concluded. At the present time we are discussing the resolution which precedes the war appropriation bill, and until that bill is passed we should not, except for very special reasons, consider taking up the time of the house in the discussion of other matters which, though all important, are not as important as the necessity of giving an assurance to our armed forces everywhere that this House of Commons is giving its first attention to their needs. That is the line on which we have been proceeding. If we had begun by taking up external affairs and discussing policies with regard to Canada's relations with other countries, the first criticism would have come, and rightly so, from hon. gentlemen opposite, or if not from them, certainly from, those who are fighting the battles of the country. And that criticism would have been this, "Why can you not give your attention to the practical question of supplying the needs of those who are fighting the battle of freedom at the front?"
I suggested, as soon after the Easter recess as possible, after we had disposed of this measure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not say after the conclusion of the war appropriation measure.
That is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If that is what the hon. member has in mind, that is all right; but we must get on more rapidly with our programme if he expects it to be immediately after Easter, when we shall have concluded the war appropriation measure. I had hoped that we would have concluded that measure before Easter.
I should have welcomed a discussion on external affairs at a fairly early stage of the session

I would not say at the very outset- but hon. gentlemen are asking, for instance, when the budget will be brought down, that now seems to be the most urgent question at the moment. It must be an urgent question if the country wishes to have the budget brought down at an early date; but are we to delay the bringing down of the budget to discuss external affairs? These are questions which the government has to face in a practical way.
It is not correct to say that we have left until a late stage in the session the discussion of external affairs. But even if we had, as long as there was full opportunity given to discuss these matters during the session, the house could not say its members had been

denied that privilege. I am anxious to have a discussion) on external affairs at a fairly early stage of the session, but in respect of some things at the present time I cannot control my owm engagements.
As hon. gentlemen know, I expect to visit England very shortly. That may be immediately after the Easter recess, or it may be a month or two months hence, but if there is a chance I shall seek to bring on an early discussion.
You had better not make it too definite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It may be during the Easter recess; it may be a week or two after, or a month or two months after. I therefore cannot say at what time some of these matters may be taken up.
It is a forthright answer.

We have listened to a beautiful speech by the Prime Minister. I say beautiful because it has portrayed the beauties of parliament, and so forth and so on, and the Prime Minister has attempted to show us the various criticisms that might come if we act now, and so forth and so on. But we all know that it is just so many words. He spoke as though we might lose the war if we did not have a certain item passed, or that somebody would go short of his salary if we did not move quickly to vote a certain sum of money, which we all know is just so many words. These things just do not happen. The war is going on whether we sit here or not; civil servants are going to be paid whether we sit here or not; and with all due respect to the Prime Minister I might even suggest that if there was a pretty good chance of the Liberal party winning an election he would not think twice about proroguing to-morrow. Now that would not mean that the war would be lost or that some civil servants would go without money.
It would mean a change of government, though.

Let me remind the government that there is precedent for this; for if ever we wanted to get a move on in a hurry it was in 1940, just a few months after the war started. We all know what happened on January 26, 1940. Well, the war did not stop. Civil servants got their money and there was no money voted until we met late in the spring. However, we know what the Prime Minister means, and we can assure him that we want to facilitate the procedure in this house. We want to win the war, and nobody is going to act in any other manner.
So far as the principle of voting money is concerned, I think that is a thing we have to consider. My understanding is that when the government comes to parliament asking for money it is tantamount to His Majesty asking the people for money, and that at that time the representatives of the people have a right to lodge their complaints at the foot of the throne. That is my understanding of the principle involved. Therefore I say no item should be passed without members of parliament having ample opportunity to lodge complaints, though I have no objection to facilitating the work of the house by consenting to an item being passed if we are given the assurance that we may talk about it at some other time.
Dealing with this particular item I should like to ask one or two questions of the Prime Minister or the Minister of Mines and Resources; if they are not prepared to answer them at the moment I shall place them on the order paper. I understand that the large proportion of the refugees seeking asylum in Canada have come from the western part of the European battlefront, coming through Spain and Portugal to England and thence to North America. I understand, on the other hand, that quite a number of refugees from the eastern part of the European front have had to move over to certain sections of Asia, to Iran and India and perhaps to Turkey. I should like to know whether any of those refugees are finding asylum on this continent.
Having asked that question, would the minister mind telling the committee the procedure that should be followed when people in this country desire to have their relatives who are refugees in some other part of the world come to this country. I have a case in point which perhaps will serve as a more direct illustration. I have an inquirer who came originally from Poland. His relatives are understood to be somewhere in the east. They are destitute, and the inquirer in this country also is without money. There has been an exchange of correspondence, however, and the people here would like very much to have their relatives come to Canada. What is the procedure in a case of this kind?
It is the general impression in this country that those who have been able to gain asylum in Canada or in North America are people with some means. Of course I have no objection to any refugee coming here, but I do think something should be done to facilitate the movement of the more unfortunate, of whom there must be many, who have no money at all. If I were a refugee somewhere I should think I would feel much safer if I had my

Supply-External Affairs

pockets full of money, so it would seem only common sense to assume that the people who really need help are those with no money at all. I do wish something could be done for them.
Would the minister mind answering the question in regard to the procedure that should be followed? If he wishes me to place on the order paper a series of questions on these matters in order to give him time to look them up, I shall be pleased to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will recognize that the exigencies of war impose certain definite limitations upon what any government can do in seeking to meet the laudable wishes of many members of the community. For example, my hon. friend has referred to some persons who would like to leave India and come to Canada.
From anywhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very well; make it from anywhere. The first problem that presents itself is how and where they are going to secure the necessary transportation to bring them to Canada, with the position as it is at present on all the oceans of the world and transportation for war purposes having the priority which necessarily it must have. Definite limitations arise from that fact; one of the greatest of the problems to-day is that of transport. A great many people in the British isles would like to come to Canada; a number of people in Canada are very anxious to get back to the British isles. Not a day passes when a request does not come to the Department of External Affairs asking if transportation cannot be arranged for someone; and in nearly every case the reply has had to be that at present it is impossible to arrange any transportation. That is the first limitation, and it is one that has operated in a definite way. There have been one or two cases where something has been arranged, as for example the exchange of nationals with Japan. It was possible to make special arrangements in those cases, but- they were limited and were made under great difficulty. As to the method of procedure, I would say that inquiries should be made of the Department of Immigration, and that department will give such information as can be given at the time. I do not think I can say more than that.

There have been times, though, when shipping could be arranged. If my recollection serves me aright, shipping was arranged at one time, and we had a shipload of refugees seeking asylum in many countries. At that time we did not offer any asylum to the refugees.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is another aspect of the refugee problem I should like to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister, on which he may care to make a statement. A number of times to-day, in another connection, it has been stated that to-morrow is the last day of March. That is the day when the full effect of the white paper of 1939 comes into operation with respect to Palestine. As the Prime Minister knows, that white paper has the effect of closing the doors of Palestine to any further Jewish immigration. I realize, as the Prime Minister does, that some permits which have been issued have not been acted upon as yet; in other words I believe it will still be posable for persons holding those permits to enter Palestine if they are able to get there. Apart from that, however, the door closes to-morrow. As the Prime Minister knows, there is a good deal of feeling among members of the Jewish community in regard to this white paper. The feeling is that it is in contradiction to the Balfour declaration, which was made not only to the Jewish people of the old country but to the Jewish people of a number of countries involved in the drafting of the original Balfour declaration. Perhaps I should) qualify that a bit and not say they were involved in the drafting of the declaration; the British government consulted the allied governments of that time before the declaration was announced, and it had their concurrence. After the declaration was made, other governments, notably the congress of the United States, issued a statement in full support of the principle of the Balfour declaration. I have digressed to this extent simply to point out that although it was a British government declaration, other countries, including Canada, are concerned. In a sense a commitment was made to the people of this country, as well as to those of Great Britain and other countries.
Has the Prime Minister any information he could give the house on this point? Can he tell us whether the government of Canada has made any representations to the BritiA

government in the matter? The question has been raised in the house before, both last year andi this year, as the Prime Minister will recall. In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the (bon. member for Trinity stated the case quite fully. Now that 'the urgency of the matter has come to our attention-because to-morrow the doors of Palestine close to any further Jewish immigration-I should appreciate it if the Prime Minister would make a statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As the hon. member has just said, the agreement was one which was made by the United Kingdom, and naturally it is of very special concern to the United Kingdom government. As my hon. friend knows, there is shortly to be a meeting in London of the prime ministers from different parts of the commonwealth. This is one of the questions which I expect will be considered there. I think until that conference takes place, and there is an opportunity to confer with those who may be present, it would be wiser for me not to make any statement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If the Prime Minister could say to-day that if the question is not on the agenda when he gets to London he will see to it that it is raised, I am sure it would mean a great deal to the Jewidh community of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Within the last day or two I have been waited upon by representatives of the Jewish community, and those who are interested in the question that has been raised, namely that of Palestine as a home for the Jew's. I believe that to-morrow again I am to meet another delegation. To those who have waited upon me I have said that it was a matter I intended to see would be considered at the meeting of prime ministers. I do not think I ought to go further than that at the present time.
It is well that my hon. friend has seen fit to add that qualification.

I am not suggesting it is true; I hope it is not. But articles such as this, if untrue, do inestimable damage to our reputation as a free and a liberty-loving country. If the statement is not true, it should be refuted. I would ask the minister to give the facts as soon as possible.

which my hon. friend has referred is one that was brought to my attention within the past week or ten days.

I understand the lady was going from Buffalo to Detroit.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury). Ann Arbor.

I do not wish to say anything further about it, but my hon. friend knows that for many years we have had legislation in Canada affecting Chinese immigration to this country, and restricting movements very greatly. In this particular case the fault did not lie with any official of the Canadian government.
Will the railway officials take it upon themselves to do that?

If my memory serves me correctly, this is the first time that refugees have been mentioned in the estimates. Therefore we have a new policy. Prior to this time refugees have been under the control of the Minister of Mines and Resources, and have been admitted under the regulations of the immigration branch. What is a refugee? What is the difference between a refugee and an ordinary immigrant? What is the difference between a refugee and an exile? That is the term used in some places. Outsiders whose transportation to Canada is facilitated or who
Supply-External Affairs

are helped to return to their country of origin are not refugees any more, nor are they exiles or immigrants or emigrants. According to the designation given by the League of Nations Society, they are evacuees.
Does the term "refugee" apply to only one race, or does it apply to all those who are coming to this country from occupied Europe? It would be well to lcnow the kind of people we are talking about, and what the money is voted for. Some people believe that those who are dealing with the problem of immigration in war time are anti-Semitic. That is not the question at all. The question is to know who is coming here and how they come here. I listened to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), who is one of the best debaters in the house, and I heard him mention refugees who have no money. If they have no money, how are they able to travel such a long distance to Canada? Some differentiation should be made between refugees, immigrants and exiles who are self-supporting and who are not self-supporting. As I say, I wonder how those who are not self-supporting can come so far to Canada and then become a charge on the country.
Canadian people are kind-hearted; they are generous; they are Christians, and they suffer because of the sufferings of others. Those of us who have read reports of the miseries of people in other parts of the world are ready to help them. But before this money is voted I think we should decide that the first immigrants to be cared for will be the Canadian boys who have fought overseas for this country and who cannot get satisfactory pensions when they come home. They should be the first immigrants to be looked after. There is no excuse for not giving priority to these boys or to these girls and women who have been in our armed forces. That is my first point.
It is pitiful to think of the men who have been in our armed forces and who cannot get pensions. How is it that we have to look after people who are not our own people? We should be ready to help to a certain extent, but I think we should look after our own people first. I shall have a lot to say when the' estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health come up. We live in a strange world here in Canada, as I said when speaking on another matter not long ago. Apparently we think more of people outside our country than we do of the people within our borders. It seems to be considered bad manners to refer to the troubles of red-blooded Canadians. Apparently we are supposed to think only of the people outside our country. That is what 
is called external affairs. It is said that people who think like that are internationally minded. Let us get down to brass tacks. Let us remember that charity begins at home. Let us not be ashamed of looking after our own people who are in distress.
Let us go back to Riviere du Loup.

It would be via Fredericton. Sometimes the hon. member for York-Sunbury speaks quite sensibly and it is unfortunate that he should spoil his reputation by making wise cracks which are rather hard to justify at times. I regret that a man of his age and ability has not given this problem the consideration it deserves. I would not want to joke about a matter like this; it is too serious, because it concerns the future of this country. There may be jibes from hon. gentlemen; others may laugh or cast aspersions-that is their right and I will not complain, speaking from my own point of view. But 1 do regret that the hon. gentleman does not give more serious attention to a problem of this scope.
We have an empire parliamentary association made up of people who hope to be the future rulers of the world. I see one hon. gentleman who probably expects to be the minister of external affairs when his leader comes to power. He is internationally minded. The leader of the C.C.F. is internationally minded. He thinks that Canada will play a great role among the nations of the world, and with that I agree, although I am not as internationally minded as he is. But Canada cannot play a great role among the nations of the world unless we have a definite Canadian policy. The principle of numerical strength seems to apply to any meetings attended by Canada, and the result is that the voice of Canada is not always heard. The Canadian policy should be drafted at home. When international meetings are held, representatives of Canada should be able to explain just what our policy is.
This item covers the portion of expenses of the intergovernmental committee on refugees. Who sits on that intergovernmental committee? Is it a Canadian committee made up of representatives of all the provinces, or is it a committee made up of representatives of the different governments in the world? When we know that, we shall be in position to ask what happened at the conference held last year in Bermuda at which Canada was not represented, and rightly so. No definite conclusions were reached at that meeting.
We do not want to see any trouble caused to Jews or to any other race, but we do not

Supply-External Affairs
want to see Canada run by foreigners and outsiders, by men from Geneva or other places who occupy key positions in Canada and who boss Canadian affairs. This should be of great concern to us all. How is it possible to have a Canadian policy when the Department of External Affairs is composed of men from all parts of the world who act as advisers to the government on international issues? I admit that a man may come from outside Canada and still be a good Canadian. On many occasions I have said that some of the people born in the British isles or other places outside of Canada were better Canadians than those born in the country. But those people have the happiness of this country at heart. What they had in view was to serve this country before all others. The people who are afraid of the propaganda of these international organizations for refugees, those who bend before those who take the lead in this movement, now say that the situation in the province of Quebec is unfortunate, that the French-Canadians are against the Jews, that the French-Canadians are against one class of the population, that they do not want refugees who want to take control of the whole country. That is not true at all. But how is it possible for men who have no experience of Canada to come here and take control of all the important positions there are, not only in the civil service, but in the government?
So long as a man comes here from outside, he is apparently all right. I remember the case of Alexander Gunn, that great expert who was called from London, not as a refugee, not as an immigrant, not as an exile, but as a kind of missionary from the British government, to tell us, to tell all Canadians what were essential positions and what were nonessential positions from which men should be transferred to the essential positions. That man was called here for the very reason that more importance is attached in this country to anything said by an outsider than to what is said by a good Canadian.
Not only that, but you know what happened with respect to the anti-nazi camp at Sherbrooke. I spoke about that last year. After Dunkirk there was a panic in England and there was a round-up of all men of central European origin who were in London. They were sent here and the government put them in a concentration camp. Think of that- anti-nazis being put in a concentration camp in Canada. I asked the Minister of National Defence last year if he knew anything about it, and he said no. But afterwards what did I see? I saw that an order in council had been
passed precisely to give a chance to these then who had entered Canada contrary to the provisions of the Immigration Act. They should have been returned to their country of origin. As I said to the Minister of Mines and Resources two or three years ago, where shall we send refugees from occupied Europe who have entered Canada illegally? There was an uproar of laughter at my question and it was not answered. I should like it answered.
I have no racial animosity in speaking as I do. I have a profound love of my country and of my fellow-citizens, and I am ready to accept the rule of any Canadian in any high post in this country, but I deny any outsider the right to boss us in this country. I think the man who has lived his whole life in this country has the right to attain to the highest positions of responsibility in this country, but I deny to the newcomer and a migratory bird the same right.
Moreover, I learned some time ago that a person who sits in the other house used to have fits when she spoke of refugees, and it was said to me by someone in authority that she cried, that she thought only of the refugees. Well, if one is to be in the other house to represent only those who do not belong to this country, there should be some means of stopping that. I know whereof I speak.
I hope, sir, that in the future those who speak of international affairs and the like will have a programme ready to submit to the house, and be ready to explain what is their stand on any item for the purpose which appears in the estimates. If some of those refugees were not so rugged when they come to this country, if they were not taking possession of Canada when they come here, they would be tolerated, but the man with the worst possible manners that I have ever seen was a millionaire refugee from France. He was eating in the dining room of the Ritz-Carlton in Montreal, and everyone was shocked by his bad manners. He was powerfully rich; he belonged to one of the richest families in the world, but I have never seen before a man who looked like him. Which means that it is not only wealth that we should bring here. It is all right to help other peoples. We have been giving billions of dollars to help other countries, and we have no objection to helping other peoples. We will do our best for them, as much as we can. But we must look after our own people in the first place, and then we must be very careful that we are not ruled by the bold refugees who come here from outside to take hold of this country, or then we shall be slaves in our own country. We cannot have that.
Supply-External Affairs

What is the policy of other peoples? What do they do for Canada, these refugees? When I asked for help here for poor settlers who need help for themselves and their children, I could not get it. The Indians get help, but I could not get it for my own people, and I do not see how the refugees can get it. I hope that the government will take that into consideration and will not press further for the passing of this item.
The United States is a large country, and it puts quotas on immigration. But so-called anti-nazis are sent here and we accept them. They jump the fence and get in. They were accepted here in spite of the laws of the land. There will be no end to it if we do not put a stop to it.
One other thing I will mention in passing. Why is it that those young men who were not originally residents of this country, young men who have come here from all over as guests in this country, are not subjected to the mobilization act? Why is that? If I am told that they are, I say that a number of those boys who have come here since the passing of the mobilization act have no trouble at all in continuing at their civilian work and are not called up by the registrars of the various military districts. That also is stupid. How is it that a man who comes here for shelter is not bound by the ordinary obligations of a Canadian citizen? I know that by speaking like this I shall scandalize some virgin souls who do not like plain talk about these matters. In external affairs we have gone far backwards. I regret it, and I hope that the policy of the government will be so changed as to be along the same lines as-
I wonder whether the hon. member would allow me to ask a question?
Surely.
If he were a member of the British house, what would his attitude be to Viscount Bennett, who was bom in New Brunswick and schooled in this country?
That question is too easy!

There is a certain attitude of reciprocity as between England, Scotland, Ireland and Canada, and I am curious to know what the hon. member's position would be under these circumstances toward Viscount Bennett.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot reply to the hon. member for Fort William, because this item refers to refugees and he is speaking of an evacuee.
I hope that the matter to which I have been referring will be considered on its merits. I appreciate the kindness of the committee in

listening to my views, which I express in all earnestness. I trust that the government will not be too quick in pressing the adoption of this item, for the reasons I have mentioned, and many others which I will give in due course.
I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister that, since there is a question which I desire to ask the Minister of Mines and Resources, who at the moment is not in his place, and which-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is trying to get a little lunch. He has not had any yet. The cabinet meeting lasted until three o'clock.
I hope that the Prime Minister is not taking umbrage at what I am saying.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no, but my hon. friend was drawing attention to the absence of the minister, and I was saying that the minister had been to my knowledge in the cabinet until nearly three o'clock this afternoon and has had no lunch. He slipped off for a minute to get a bite to eat.
I am not raising any question about the minister going out to his lunch.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend drew attention to his absence from the chamber, and I am giving him the reason.
My right hon. friend need not be so touchy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not touchy, but part of my duty is to defend my colleagues during their absence, and when my hon. friend puts on Hansard the statement that a particular minister is not here, and my hon. friend knows the significance of that, I am giving him the explanation.

I merely innocently rose to ask the Minister of Mines and Resources a question. I cannot ask the question if he is not here, but if the Prime Minister wants to answer it I will tell him- what it is. He may clear it up and the matter will then be concluded.
When the hon. member for York-Sunbury rose in his place to bring to the attention of the Minister of Mines and Resources the incident of an American girl travelling from New York to Ann Arbour, Michigan, I thought the minister did not make a clear explanation of the situation, because there is a serious aspect of this particular complaint. I wish to put on the record one sentence in connection with the report which was published in the New Republic, and which was

Supply-External Affairs
mentioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury during the debate. That publication refers to-
. . . this piece of startling governmental stupidity and brutality (which) occurs over and over; No American citizen who looks like a Chinese, we are told, is allowed to pass through Canadian territory on an American train even though the points of departure and arrival are in the United States. Canada has a good record in this war; and it is a little startling to find her deliberately going out of the way to insult and humiliate citizens of an allied country, the United States.
The reason why I rose at this time was to give the Minister of Mines and Resources, or the Prime Minister if he chooses-perhaps the Prime Minister is the one to do it-an opportunity of making a categorical denial of the entire statement and a proper explanation of what happened, because I do not think what has been said goes far enough, in view of the serious charge which is made in a United States magazine with a wide circulation. I believe the Prime Minister and every member of the house wants to repudiate any suggestion that this country would treat nationals of another country in the manner alleged, and in my opinion the Minister of Mines and Resources should have gone farther than simply to say that no Canadian immigration official was involved; he should have told the whole story. What I intended to suggest at the beginning of my remarks was that the item might be allowed to stand until the Minister of Mines and Resources returned to the chamber. If the Prime Minister desires to make an explanation, that is satisfactory to me; but the article should not go unchallenged, because it contains a reflection on our relationship to other countries, and I should like to see the matter satisfactorily cleared up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The minister, I thought, made it quite clear that such action as was taken was not by any Canadian government official, and that any such action on the part of any of its officials would not be countenanced for one moment by our government. Possibly the minister, for reasons which he had better explain himself, deemed it inadvisable to place the responsibility where, perhaps, it exclusively belongs. I will allow him to answer that part himself. So far as the government is concerned I can assure my hon. friend that every member of the government would take the strongest exception to any action of the kind on the part of an official, and in this particular instance the government officials were wholly innocent of any such act.
Our position is one of friendship toward nations which are friendly with us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly. The incident was most regrettable.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words'to say on the question of refugees. That matter is closely connected with the immigration question. During the war we have had to admit into Canada a large nmber of so-called refugees, who have been expelled from their own country by the invader but who may wish to become permanent residents of Canada. Despite the kindheartedness of the Canadian citizens, that question is, in mj- opinion, one of very great importance and we. should not. exclude reason from our feelings. We must not forget that the post-war period will probably be marked by widespread unemployment and that we shall then have to take care of hundreds of thousands of demobilized soldiers and laid off workmen apart from those refugees and of the immigrants whom some may wish to send here.
I ask the government to take my remarks into serious consideration. I agree with what the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) has said a few moments ago, and I must say that the government has received numerous petitions and that I have also received some which indicate the general feeling in Shefford county. I ask the government, once again, to consider the question of postwar immigration and to make sure that the number of immigrants admitted is commensurate with the employment available at that time. Without any doubt, we shall then have very serious problems to solve in connection with the Canadians who will have to be provided for. I ask the government that before they take care of European refugees, they provide for Canadian-born citizens.

In view of some of the remarks that have been made with regard to this small item, I should like to be heard. The hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) commented that the matter should be considered on its merits, and of course with that statement I entirely agree.
Let us see what the problem is that we are considering on its merits. I understand that an intergovernmental committee has been set up to consider at some length continuously a problem which is on the hands of all the nations of the world, those of good will at all events, those on the united nations side, with respect to people fleeing the wrath of the nazi murderers in Germany and other occupied territories in Europe.
Supply-External Affairs

My good friend t(he hon. member for Temisoouata says that charity should begin at home. Of course that is right, but unfortunately he has not finished the quotation: It should not stay at home. The remarks madie by that hon. member reminded me of the little couplet:
Me and my wife, John and his wife.
Us four and no more.
It is a matter of judgment. It is true that, as he says, our first concern in this country is the returned men from the front, that they have priority on all occasions, and that of course they be given reasonable treatment in the matter of pensions. But it can hardly be contended that the question of giving a sufficiency in pensions to our returned men in any way depends upon or is influenced or affected by the S5,000 appropriation in order that Canada may take her place and her proper place among other nations in doing the right thing by poor people.
It does seem to me, however, looking at the matter entirely from the point of view of -the boys who are returning, that were we in this chamber to take a miserable, mean attitude, that charity stays at home, exclusively in Canada, and that we cannot afford $5,000 in order that Canada should take her place on an intergovernmental committee, these boys returning here would blush with shame that they come from Canada rather than from some of the other nations -that are playing a proper part.
The hon. member for Temiscouata said that Canadians are a kind-hearted people, and that is true. We are a self-respecting nation, and it. would not, it seems to me, be in keeping with our self-respect if we even questioned this amount, much less if we rejected it.
I compliment the government upon taking its proper place on this international committee for the handling of this modt important world problem. If the item is to be criticized at all, it is only because it is so small.

I just wish to add a word along the line taken by the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Roebuck). In bis part of Toronto and in my part as well there are people of all races, and I have found sons and daughters of all races, no matter what their language was, no matter where they came from, rendering good service to the country. I, too, congratulate the government upon carrying out its agreement, in fact on entering into an agreement even in a small way, and it is only in a small way, to relieve the unparalleled and almost unmentionable distress that refugees
TMr. Roebuck.]
of all races in Europe -have gone through. It is a small item which does not mean very much in money, but I am happy to support it.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The next item is one which relates to the Department of Finance, the estimates of which have not thus far been called. If hon. gentlemen wish to obstruct or to delay the proceedings of the house-

Do not
use that word "obstruct."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not saying that they will, -but if anyone wishes to delay the proceedings of the house, the business of the country, he may take exception at this moment to our discussing on a Thursday, when Mr. Speaker leaves the chair without question put an item in a department that has not already been called. I am obliged to leave the chamber shortly and I wish to make a statement on this before withdrawing. Hon. members * will have noticed that since the beginning of the session the government has sought on a Monday, or Tuesday or Wednesday to have the different departments called in as expeditious an order as possible, but we have been prevented time and again, particularly in the last two weeks, from getting any additional departments into supply. It has not been the fault of the government that all departments have not been called up to this moment. It has been owing to the fact I have mentioned, that motions have been put which have made that impossible. I do not take exception to that; that is the right of the opposition.
I hope you are not referring to the opposition, because we did not raise any questions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I regard everyone who is not for the government as being opposed to it.

If that is the situation
the Prime Minister had better withdraw his remarks about the opposition having brought in amendments to the motion for supply, because we have not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I regard those who are not for the government as opposed to it, and when I speak of the opposition I do not mean my hon. friend only. I mean particularly some of those hon. gentlemen who belong to other groups and who have been-

Do not
class us with them, please.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My own belief is that there should be simply one government and one opposition. I think it is a mistake having the house divided into the government and its supporters and three or four oppositions, so that each time one of that number speaks the other three feel that they must also put in their oars or say something.
In the years I have been in parliament there have always been, just before the beginning of the new fiscal year, some estimates brought down in the nature of further supplementary estimates to cover small amounts that may be outstanding to meet accounts for the current year. I have never once seen the house refuse to give unanimous consent to the consideration of these estimates on the score of any rule that may appear in the rules of procedure of the house, and I hope that we may take it as assumed that hon. members opposite of all parties are prepared to allow the government to proceed with a discussion of any items that may appear on this supplementary list.

Speaking
on behalf of the official opposition, I wish to assure the Prime Minister at once that no objection will be taken to any item of any department which has not yet been called, but I would point out to him that he has a good many departments in already. As far as my recollection goes, he has more departments in than is the case in the ordinary session of parliament. It is the right and the duty of the opposition to see that too many departments are not brought in too soon. My hon. friend knows that, and nobody was more dexterous in preventing that sort of thing than the right hon. gentleman when he sat on this side, and especially some of his henchmen who sit around him, in days gone by. I have reason to remember that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Speaking of the rights of the opposition and of the government, I would say to my hon. friend that the government has a perfect right, once in supply, to call an item in every department if it so desires. There is no rule of the house which says the opposition has the right to prevent the government from obtaining supply in any way it can, consistent with the rules. It has been to help meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen opposite that the government has not called every department once it has been in supply. I should like to have that clearly understood. Once the house is in supply the government has a perfect right to call any item in any department it pleases; and if we had wished to stand strictly on our rights, the first day the house met we could have called an 100-127
item in each department and been free to go into supply any Thursday or Friday on the estimates of any department. But that is not the way in which business can be carried on as between a government and an opposition.
May I take advantage of this opportunity to point out what I think is in the interests of all hon. members, namely, that we cannot make progress unless each member assumes a real responsibility and restricts on his own part the amount of time to be taken in discussion. If this afternoon the Chairman had ruled strictly, as I think he should have done-if he will not mind my saying so -this discussion might have been held down to the simple question of whether a small amount still owing by Canada to an international organization should be paid. The broad discussion in regard to immigration, refugees and the like, has not been strictly relevant to the item before us. The time to take up those matters would have been when the main estimates are being discussed.
But the Prime Minister will agree that this is a new item; it is not a further item.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is an item which has arisen during the year, which there has not been a chance to meet before this; it belongs to the current year. In a word what I want to say is this. Hon. members are asking, and rightly, that we should shortly begin a discussion on external affairs, that we should bring down the budget, and that other measures should be brought down; yet discussions such as that which has taken place this afternoon make it wholly impossible to do any of these things. We have been sitting for two hours, but up to the present we have passed only one item. I think, without injury to any living soul, the whole lot of them might have been passed in ten minutes. I am perfectly certain that is what, in similar circumstances, they would have done in the British parliament. There is a vast amount of legislation still to be brought before the house, and before we get much further with the session hon. members are going to be asking the government, " Cannot this be expedited; cannot that be expedited?" This is the time for expedition, if it is to amount to anything in the long run.
If the Prime Minister does not mind, may I suggest that the estimates are not going through faster largely because of his own attitude in the matter.

Order. There is absolutely nothing before the committee; no item has been called. The dis-

Supply-Finance

cussion that has been going on has taken place between the calling of items. I should like to know what item to call.
Item 421.
Very well; 421.
421. Departmental administration - further amount required, $76,200.
I understood that we were talking on item 421.
That has just been called.

There was a discussion as to the propriety of taking up this item at all. We are not objecting to it, but my hon. friend would like to speak to that point. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, this house might stand on its rights and refuse to recognize this item at all, because as yet the Department of Finance has not been put into supply. We are not going to do that, of course, but at the same time I think my hon. friend has a right to discuss the point, which he was rising to do.

As a member of this
house, Mr. Chairman, I object to being lectured by the Prime Minister or anyone else. The right hon. gentleman rose and very properly drew to the attention of the opposition the fact that they could have refused to allow this item to come in, because the Department of Finance has not as yet been brought into supply. But he did not simply make the statement and leave it to the opposition to agree or not to agree. I am satisfied that the opposition would have agreed, but he went on and on and on, lecturing hon. members about their duties in the house; he went on to tell us that the government had the right to bring in all the departments on the first day of the session, after the estimates were introduced. Of course that is so, but it would be so only if the opposition allowed that to be done. The opposition could carry on a discussion for weeks, and under those conditions the government would not be able to bring in anything at all. I have said time and again, as the Prime Minister has said, that if we are to make progress here we must discipline ourselves and agree, as among the various groups, how much discussion shall take place on various subjects. I am absolutely in accord with that idea. The attitude of the Prime Minister reminds me of a statement which the late Henry Labouchere is said to have made in regard to the late Mr. Gladstone,
(The Chairman.]
who used to lecture the British House of Commons in somewhat the same way. He said he did not mind the old man, as he called him, having the ace of trumps up his sleeve every time, but he did object to the old man saying that God Almighty had put it there. That is the way I feel in regard to these matters. Let the Prime Minister put the point to hon. members, and if it is put fairly nicely, as the right hon. gentleman can put it.if he wishes, I am quite satisfied that we shall agree and let the item go through.

Let me point out to the Prime Minister what the hon. member for Vancouver East omitted to say. I think if Hansard were to be checked it would be found that the Liberals, including the Prime Minister, have had more to say than perhaps all the rest of us combined.

429. To provide an additional amount, and under the same terms and conditions, to that *provided under vote 475 of the Appropriation Act No. 5, 1943, for transportation and living expenses of members of the House of Commons during the Easter recess, 1943-further amount required, $250.

Although this is a vote for merely $250, I believe it is the only place at which I could make the observations I wish to make-and perhaps what I am about to say will not be any too popular. However, the present high taxation imposed upon incomes is affecting members of the House of Commons to the point where, unless they have certain expenses paid, this parliament will result in a rich man's parliament. I say that because, while some members have other interests, such as professions or businesses, quite a number make the business of being members of parliament a full-time job. In so doing they have no other income.
I am suggesting that if only a slight investigation were made it would be discovered that some members of parliament who attend parliament, with all the expenses involved- and they amount to a considerable sum, because a member has a certain kind of life he must lead-have to get along on a very small amount of money. I know, in fact, that some members have to draw on their indemnities long before they are due.
I understand I have some small support, because I have read, in some, of Canada's leading daily papers, several editorials in which the same view has been expressed. I believe the country is gradually realizing the truth of what I have said. Especially is this true in war time, when taxation is high, and when the work of the member of parliament, somehow or another, is doubled. In war time he must attend to many things which in peace time he need not attend to. For instance, I have in mind particularly members who represent large constituencies, some of which are two or three hundred miles in diameter. A member in such a constituency may be requested to address a Red Cross or

Supply-Legislation-House oj Commons
salvage meeting, or to appear before a board of trade or a council, and! to do so 'he must travel the width of 'his constituency. Nevertheless he receives no out-of-pocket expenses. He has to do this on the indemnity he receives, one which, in reality, is supposed to indemnify him against loss of time during a parliamentary session.
I believe it would be only fair if the government were to give some consideration to this matter. We want to bear our fair share of the burden of taxation, but the situation is such that I think we are bearing more than our share, because no consideration is given to our expenses outside the session. I believe it would be only fair if the government were to. allow members of parliament a certain, amouat to cover expenses involved in carrying on their work. I am not alone when I make these observations, because I think almost every member of parliament agrees with what I have said, and I would urge that the government do something about the matter.
What dioes the horn, member think would be a fair amount for expenses?

I do not know; I am afraid I cannot answer that. I do not think any member of parliament wants to make money out of it; but I am of opinion that some regulation could be arrived at which would be fair to all members. On the one hand we may find' a city member, the length and breadth of whose constituency would not cover more than a mile or so. On the other hand we find another member who must travel a couple of hundred miles to cover his constituency. From one end of my constituency to the other is a distance of 200 miles. The people at one end of my constituency have just as much right to my services as any organization in the constituency of a city member, but I may have to travel a couple of hundred miles while the other fellow needs only to hop on a street car.
What would the expenses here in Ottawa be worth?

I do not know about that. If a member of parliament cannot bring his family to Ottawa he must keep two homes going. No member can live in Ottawa and keep up the position he should at less than what it costs him to live at home, even though he has his family here with him. I am sure if the people were aware of these expenses they would not object to the government allowing hon. members out-of-pocket expenses.
TMr. Hansell.]
Mr. O'BRIEN: I should like to approach this problem from another point of view. Two or three sessions ago I referred to the matter of taxation, and I was criticized severely by the press, it being intimated I was trying to avoid the payment of the tax. This time I should like to approach the matter from the constitutional point of view. Up to a certain time members of parliament received indemnities, but now they receive salaries. I submit it is entirely unconstitutional for a member to be sitting here representing the people and receiving a salary. Apart altogether from the matters referred to by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I submit that a most serious situation exists in this parliament at the present time. It should be cleared up. If the tax is to be taken off the indemnity, it should be done by an amendment to the House of Commons Act, which originally gave hon. members their indemnities.

I should like to associate myself briefly with the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) and with those of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. O'Brien). If a member of the House of Commons is paid an indemnity for his services, either the indemnity was too large before the war or, if it was not, it is too small to-day. Because of added taxation, the increase in the cost of living and the extra work that must be performed as a consequence of the war, it would seem to me that the indemnity received by hon. members to-day is much too small.

Item agreed to.
iSO. To provide an additional amount required for expenses of the special committee on war expenditures under the same terms and conditions as provided under vote 476 of the Appropriation Act No. 5, 1943-further amount required, $1,600.

My remarks will be brief, but they would be much longer if it were not for the circumstances. In my opinion this is a good example of wasted money. It is not very often that I make a charge as bluntly as that, but that is what this actually means. Apart altogether from the uselessness of certain parts of the work of this committee, which I am not going to deal with because I have referred to it before, the main reason for this expenditure is the fact that this committee was set up in the dying days of the last session. Therefore it had to sit between sessions and incurred expenses which had to be paid by the taxpayers of Canada.
I doubt if there is anything we can do at this stage except to protest, as I have protested before, against this situation. When this committee was set up so late in the last session

Supply-Legislation-House of Commons
every hon. member must have realized that it would mean money out of the taxpayers' pockets. Had the war expenditures committee been able to sit while the house was in session there would have been no need for these extra expenses. The Prime Minister is not at the moment in the house, so that I shall not press for further details. The most charitable view that can be taken of this expenditure is that it is attributable directly to the situation I have described. I simply wish to make this vigorous and vehement protest against what I think is a waste of public funds.
That is your opinion.
I think my opinion ought to be heard in the House of Commons and I do not want the hon. member to challenge it.

This committee was
appointed some three years ago to carry on a definite task in the darkest hours of the war, but it has outlived its public usefulness. The committee and the system have been weighed in the balance and found wanting. In saying that, I do not wish to reflect upon the hon. gentlemen who compose the committee. It was a very good body of men. However, I protest against the useless system. In the olden days we used to have an auditor general, a Mr. McDougall, who made a great name for himself because of the way in which he checked expenditures. He had the power to veto expenditures which he considered were not within the four corners of the law as it then was. But then the great war came along and that practice was discontinued. Last session I read a letter from the auditor general in which he stated that he had no power to investigate any account incurred under the war appropriation bill which called for four billion dollars. Last year the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) referred to this, as did the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and myself. A comptroller of the treasury was appointed. This officer is a civil servant appointed by the Minister of Finance and under his control. He passes upon all accounts which come within the four corners of the resolution upon the order paper, which is divided into paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d). Would any business firm conduct a four billion dollar business like that, without any checks and balances? I do not object to the trips that the committee take, although they are not authorized to take Cook's tours all 'over Canada. I do not object to that. I have not been able to take any myself. But I am glad that the members see Canada and learn something about the country. It may in the end save some money. But there is a war on and
the public think we should have a system of checks and balances over our expenditures. I have had many business men write me on this
subject.
The public usefulness of the committee has gone. As I suggested the. year before last, we should change our system. At the other end of this building we have what is technically called another place, a very good body of men; sometimes they call it a house. It is not a house at all; it is only half of parliament; you would not call it a house. But it is there, without war work to do, although willing to do it. Why could they not be given the opportunity of doing some more useful work? I read a report of its meeting the other day. They said prayers, took in four new members from Quebec, and then adjourned-and they call that a day's work. The whole business of parliament should be reconstructed and divided in war time. In England, three years before the war, they had long debates on this subject of parliamentary reform, and they reformed the upper chamber and gave it more legislative work to do, looking into accounts and all that kind of thing. They have a real system of checks and balances.
When the Tupper government left office in 1896 our expenditures were S36,000,000 a year, and under Laurier they were 837,000,000. We are now spending that much in three or four days, and when the taxpayer gets his bills he is beginning to wonder about all this expenditure in the fifth year of the war. I do not object to members of the committee taking Cook's tours to the sun or the moon if we are getting value for it, but it was not the intention that the committee should travel around the way it does. They should sit down like the British committee and go over the expenditures. The British committee gets results and changes; it has a big staff of accountants and outside auditors checking the expenditures, and it meets the whole year round and gets some place. But the committee here sits one day and then departs to Montreal or for parts unknown, and then some of them go by aeroplane to Halifax. Let them take all the trips they like. I am not objecting to that. What I am objecting to is the system under which we spend over four billion dollars a year, without any check on it. Any large departmental store that had such a system would go bankrupt; with everybody spending money just as he likes. A letter was read in the house by me not long ago in which the auditor general said he had not control over some expenditures.
The time has come to take action. I move,. Mr. Chairman, that this item be reduced to'
