one dollar. That will give this committee an opportunity to express its dissatisfaction with the conduct of the war expenditures committee. It holds its meetings behind closed doors, like the Star Chamber. I asked in the house the other day if a private member could go into the committee and the answer was: no; you cannot go into the committee. The doors are closed and locked and no private member can get in. But in 1923 when the Canadian National railway estimates were under consideration I asked the late respected Bight Hon. George Graham if a private member could go into the select committee on railways and shipping and ask questions, and he announced that any private member could go into the committee and ask questions on any railway matter in which he was interested.
Certainly a change is needed in the system. We should get some public-spirited business men in Canada to act as a committee or royal commission and go over the accounts, and make recommendations for retrenchment looking toward a better business system. That would strengthen the hands of the Minister of Finance. I advocated in 1924 and 1925 that we should adopt the municipal system, and the hon. member for Wellington South has been taking that up in the last three or four years. That would enable us to reduce and strike out various items of the estimates. But that policy has not been adopted. We follow the old practice of two hundred years ago under which a minister resigns if his estimates are reduced. To show disapproval I move that this item be reduced to one dollar.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the members of the committee I think a word should be said. Members of the committee and I are getting fairly well fed up with the constant charges of Cook's tours, giving the impression that the different inspection trips made by members of the committee are not made at their own expense. I want to say positively that every trip made at any time by the war expenditures committee has been made at the personal expense of the members of the committee. The committee members reecive a per diem allowance of $12 for every day they are away from home at Ottawa or otherwise on committee business, when the house is not sitting. When the house is sitting and trips are made the members make them in their own time and at their own expense, and no expense account of any kind is payable to any member of the committee when he goes to Vancouver or Halifax or any other place in Canada.

The hon. member for Broadview says that the Canadian committee is not functioning as the British committee is functioning. In his very next breath he complains of in camera meetings. The British committee has held all its meetings ever since the outbreak of war in camera. He cannot have it both ways. My hon. friend knows better than to make a statement of that kind. Time and again in debates on the subject this house has been told that the Canadian committee is functioning as nearly as can be after the manner in which the British committee is functioning. One feature of the Britsih committee is the fact that all its meetings are held in camera. Our meetings are held in camera, not that we have anything to conceal, but simply that we can better do our job in in camera meetings.
The hon. member for Broadview also stated that the British committee employed accountants, auditors and the like. I took the trouble to have an interview with the chairman of the British committee when he visited this country a year ago, and I was told by him that the committee does not make a practice of hiring accountants and auditors, but is doing exactly as we are doing here. When they need professional assistance or the help of accountants they call them in just as we call in men who are already in the employ of the government in the various departments to assist us in our work. The members of the war expenditures committee were asked to take this work on as a war task and we have approached it entirely from that viewpoint. It is not an easy thing for a member of that committee to spend weeks and months of his time in between long sessions doing this work, which is quite often tedious and tiresome, but I wish to assure the committee that we are approaching it from the point of view of a war duty. We are trying to do our best, and while I do not mind fair criticism I do not like this constant unfair criticism as though the committee simply were going on joy rides and the like.

I was sorry that the leader of the opposition spoke in the way he did about the war expenditures committee. In 1941 this committee was set up, I would say at the request of the leader of the opposition of the day. I recall speeches he made at that time telling us about the war 'expenditure committee in Great Britain, and that during war time members of parliament should devote some of their time toward assisting the war effort, and that to set up a war expenditures committee here would be one fine way to help the country

Supply-Legislation-Home of Commons
in this respect. That year the committee was set up at an early date. They sat until the close of the session, by which time they found that the field they had to cover was so large that it would be well to do what was done in Britain, namely, to sit the year around. The government at the end of the session brought in a supplementary estimate of 825,000 to pay a living allowance to members who during the recess would sit on the committee. That committee sat from July 7, 1941, to some time in September; that is, although it had sat during the session it continued its sittings afterwards. The following year it was again set up at any early date and functioned during the session, and a supplementary estimate of $30,000 was passed at the end of the session to permit sittings during the recess. That fall the committee sat for two and one-half months or thereabouts. The members were not paid any expenses other than an allowance of $15 per diem.
Less taxes.

The $30,000 was expended and no further vote was asked for. At that time members of the opposition did not criticize these two estimates. They eon-ceded that it was a good committee, and that it was useful to the government to have a committee of that kind, because the reports it produced served as advice and as a check to the defence departments and the Department of Munitions and Supply, helping them to find ways and means of curbing expenses.
Last year the committee was set up at a late date, but that was not the reason why it sat during the recess. It sat the two previous years during the recess. Another supplementary estimate for $30,000 was voted.
As the hon. member who spoke before me has pointed out, travelling expenses are not paid to the members. Last year, I believe, they received $12 a day when they were on committee work in Ottawa.
I disagree completely with the leader of the opposition when he says that this committee has no useful purpose. If he had experience in that committee; if he knew the work which is done there and followed the procedure, he would find that it is a useful organism of government. Members of the opposition say that it has lost its use because it sits in camera. My goodness, we went over that objection in 1941, 1942, 1943, and it has come back this year. We are convinced and the government is convinced that the committee could not do its work properly if it sat in public. Much of the information given is of a secret nature. We can advise the govern-

ment as to what should be done to try to economize on some of the expenditures. I have sat on that committee for over two years, and I am still convinced that it is useful and that we should continue to follow the same procedure as we have followed hitherto. Furthermore, I believe the committee should sit during the recess, although it has been appointed early in the session. If one glances over the formidable list of expenditures made by the government in the prosecution of the war effort, it seems evident that this committee should be continuously looking into these expenses and advising the government thereon.

This committee, I believe, is one of the best committees which has ever been set up in this house. One reason is that each year since the committee has been set up, all hom. members are advised that if any irregularities have come to their notice in their constituencies it is hoped that [DOT]they will take the matter up with the committee. Every year I 'have had a letter from the chairman to that effect, and any time in my territory, which is a big one, irregularities are reported to me, I forward particulars of the complaint to the committee for investigation. I am wholly in favour of the committee being maintained. It is a great help to the individual member, and) a great advantage to the general public who are thus enabled to put grievances before a, committee of parliament.

I wish to say one word before the item passes, and that is with reference to what was said by the hon. member for Broadview. I got the impression that in his view this committee was the only agency which stood between the taxpayer and1 anyone who was spending money, and that it was the only check which was made on the public accounts in so far as war expenditures were concerned. If that is the effect of what the hon. member said, I believe he is entirely in error. I have before ,me the combined public accounts in their new form for 1943. My hon. friend suggested, I believe, that war expenditures were not under the auditor general, and that this committee was the only checking agency in regard to war expenditures which was available for the benefit of the taxpayer. I would refer my hon. friend to pages 8 and 9 of part II of the public accounts for 1943. There he will find not simply the ordinary expenses but the special expenditures and the war appropriations, all set out on those two

pages, and at the bottom appears the certificate of the official who, the hon. member says, has nothing to do with these war expenditures. That certificate reads:
The accounts of expenditure, which are associated with the foregoing statement, have been examined under my direction, and subject to the relative observations in my report to the House of Commons made in accordance with the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, I certify as the result of my audit that the statement is correct.
That is signed "Watson Sellar, Auditor General".
I hope my hon. friend will be relieved by *that of 'his misapprehension that the committee is the only' form of check which the public have.
I do not think I need add anything at the moment to -what- has been said about the committee and its work. For some reason or another the work of the committee is minimized by some hon. members, particularly by the leader of the opposition and the opposition generally. I do not understand [DOT]why they reiterate that it is not doing effective work because it is sitting in camera. That is just an instance of how .the repetition of a fallacy develops in the minds of some people the idea that it is the truth. As a matter of fact, this committee has done exceedingly valuable work. It has been stated time and time again that it is set up and functions exactly as the committee at Westminster does, and that statement has been verified in interviews with those who have had to do with the committee's work at Westminster and know the procedure which is adopted there. The question being raised on this particular item with regard to expenses is a reflection on the committee, because, as has been pointed out, travelling expenses are paid by the committee members themselves. I do not think the committee needs any defence at my hands; its members, and in particular the chairman, are quite capable of taking care of themselves; but I simply wish to assure them that the opinion expressed in some quarters with regard to their work is not held by the people of Canada generally or by the great majority of the members of this house. They work diligently, and while they cannot go over all accounts, at the same time they provide a means of checking on certain accounts and no one knows where they will strike next. All of that helps toward the proper keeping of public accounts and the maintenance of regularity in public expenditures.

I rose particularly to put on record the real situation with regard to the check provided by the auditor general not only in connection with ordinary expenditures, but in connection with war expenditures as well.

I do not rise to discuss the work of the war expenditures committee particularly. I do not think it would be wise for us to turn down the appropriation since it is for work that has already been accomplished, for expenditures that have already been incurred. For that reason I think this committee should pass this item.
As regards the work of the war expenditures committee itself, having been a member of that committee the first year it sat, 1942, I am quite convinced that it can render an important 'service. I am also of opinion that much of the reason for holding the committee meetings in camera has disappeared, and now that the war work has been got well under way there is every reason why these hearings should be held in public. There are certain matters that should not be divulged in public and they could be discussed in camera. It has been said that possibly one reason why the meetings were held as they were was that we could get more information from subordinates in departments. There is a way in which that can be remedied. A man coming before the committee can be sworn- I do not know whether that is done-and when he gives evidence he will give evidence of that which he knows, and does not hold anything back. I pass that on to the members of the committee as my own opinion. I do not think we should hold up the item.

DEPARTMENT OP NATIONAL REVENUE Income tax divisiontiSS. District offices-further amount required, $138,500.

Will the Minister of National Revenue consider putting in a branch office in Peterborough, and perhaps in other places as well? Other members may want offices in their ridings, but we have a large industrial city, and with income tax papers as they are at present, though the forms are supposed to be very simple, I believe that even some of the income tax officers would find it difficult to make up some of them.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
The matter will, of
course, receive consideration, but at the present time the difficulty of securing qualified accountants militates against opening up new offices. It would be difficult to get sufficient qualified staffs to man any more offices than we have at present. It is quite difficult to keep up the staffs in the offices we already have.

I made a suggestion to the Minister of Munitions and Supply with regard to muntions plants in places where that department has offices of its own. I suggested that those offices have men there to look after the income tax forms of workers in the plants. The workers in the plant at Peterborough have to make out their forms and then buy money orders and send them to Belleville along with their income tax forms. That puts a double tax on the wage-earner.
The sum of $138,500 seems a rather large amount for a supplementary vote. Would the minister be good enough to explain how it comes about that he was not able to make a closer estimate?

The increase has occurred
chiefly through the greatly increased number of taxpayers and the new method of collecting the tax. Postage alone amounts to $100,000 to take care of a very large number of additional returns that are being filed, which are collected by the district offices and sent to the head office. That is the largest item of the total amount. Travelling expenses amount to $22,000, and that again is occasioned by the increased number of taxpayers, which has caused higher travelling expenses.

This is a tremendous
amount, which appears to be an expansion of the income tax division. I would suggest that one thing that would be acceptable to perhaps 100 per cent of the people of Canada would be that the income tax division be done away with altogether.
The minister said that there was a great shortage of chartered accountants. What would be the percentage of accountants in each district office?
It varies with the size of the office. Some offices have a larger number of accountants, while in smaller offices we probably have only one or two.

How often are the district
income tax inspectors called to Ottawa to be given instructions or to get an interpretation of the income tax law? Are they all called at certain times? I ask this question because it seems to me that in some of these offices there are no two employees who can figure an account exactly the same. I suggest, therefore, that the income tax inspectors should be brought in to what one might call a school, at least once a year, and given instructions which they could impart to the employees.
That has been done. They were all in during the past year. In addition, we have three regional inspectors for central, western and eastern Canada who visit the local offices.

4S4. National film board, including the motion picture bureau-further	amount required,

For some time there has been a growing feeling that the work of the national film board has been devoted to a type of propaganda far beyond and in. excess of the reasons which brought about the creation of that board in the first instance. There has been a growing suspicion that the film board has become a propagandist for a type of socialist and foreign philosophy; heretofore it was merely an instrument of propaganda for the government. It is still an instrument of propaganda for the government, but it has become an instrument for the spreading of propaganda which is foreign to our Canadian way of life, and in a moment I shall show the minister what I mean.
I should like to point out why I regard this matter so seriously. The film has come to be the supreme vehicle of propaganda to-day. It takes precedence over the written word in the newspaper and the spoken word
Supply-War Services

on the radio. Not only does it combine the written word with visual action; it takes in also the spoken word, and it does all this in surroundings which lull the subject into a sense of confident security, and put him into a receptive frame of mind. The Wallman theory shows a direct ratio between the efficiency of the newspaper, the radio and the film; and I feel safe in predicting that, as time goes on, the newspapers of the country will have reason to appreciate fully the seriousness of what is happening. This is a most sinister situation, because they get the adolescent mind in a receptive mood, in comfortable surroundings, and spray it with an anaesthesia of propaganda which in most cases it is not capable of resisting. The function of the film board in England has been merely to assist the government and to explain various government policies. It has done excellent instructional work concerning rationing, health measures, security regulations and other matters. No doubt our film board has done similar work, but the Canadian board has stepped out of character and undertaken to promote a philosophy foreign to the Canadian philosophy.
Before continuing with this discussion, I should like to quote from an article written by one who is considered perhaps the best moving picture critic in the city of New York, appearing in this week's issue of the New Yorker and dealing with documentary films. The first part of the article deals with "Desert Victory," and the new picture, "Tunisian Victory," and then goes on with this interesting paragraph, which I shall read to the committee because I think hon. members will be interested:
Speaking of documentaries, the latest "World in Action" short is Russia's foreign policy, the strongest statement of the Russian point of view that has come from any place but the U.S.S.R. It maintains-and it will take no back-chat- that the Comintern was a protective measure, as was the German-Soviet pact, and that Russia is a youthful, zestful, oppression-hating state with a spirit that should be shared by the rest of the world. The film is typical of the "World in Action" series in its smoothness and economy 3f expression. Every foot of the film makes a point, and the editing of dozens of library shots 

news reels and Russian movies of all ages- has been canny. Russia's foreign policy toward the national film board of Canada, which makes this series, should be fairly amiable.
This publication certainly has no political animus; this is merely a factual criticism of this series, which is put out by the national film board. Perhaps the more that is known about Russia, the better; and from time to time I have advocated that a chair of Russian studies might be inaugurated at one of our universities, because this is an interesting and

veiy important social experiment. My objection is that we have a national instrument of government that is obviously putting out soviet propaganda. I feel strongly that it is not the duty of any vehicle of government to put out propaganda concerning any foreign country. The film board should be a Canadian film board and it should put out Canadian propaganda. If we have anything to sell, it is ourselves. The whole trend of this propaganda is dangerous because it is not delivered solely to adult minds. I would suggest to the minister that very careful investigation be made into the operation of this board. This is not the first time that this question has been brought up. There was another film put out called "Our Native Land". It was released by a French motion picture company in New York and released in Canada by the film! society. Paul Robeson took a prominent and leading part in that film. There is nothing wrong with the showing of a film on Soviet Russia or even showing films on anybody else's philosophy; in fact the more accurate information we can get, the better; but my objection is that it is not the function of a government-controlled operation to undertake this work, which is being done, according to the information I have.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Would the hon. member for York West be kind enough to give me the name of the picture which has offended him? work. That is my objection. I have no objection to communist propaganda. It is an interesting subject and we should know more about it. I did not intend to say anything on this matter, but the remarks of the hon. member for York West have placed most of us in the position where we should say something.
Since the present session of parliament opened, the national film board has made it possible for hon. members to assemble every Tuesday in a room in this building to get some knowledge of the work they are doing. Personally I am very well pleased with the contribution that the national film board is making toward clarifying the minds of the Canadian people with respect to what is going on in the Soviet Union. I do not agree with the statement that was made by the hon. member for York West. He said it was not the duty of a department of government to take the responsibility of clarifying the minds of the Canadian people, poisoned over a number of years, with respect to what was going on in Russia. It definitely is the government's responsibility. If it is not, whose responsibility is it? Does the hon. member for York West want to place the education of the Canadian people with regard to the affairs of one of our most important allies at this time back in the hands of those who carried on that education for the past twenty-five years? If he does, I think he is going too far. I believe that the Canadian government should have interested itself in this question many years ago. Members of this House of Commons are under a debt of gratitude to those who are conducting the operations of the national film board. They are making one of the most important educational contributions to the Canadian people (hat could be made at this time. It is definitely the responsibility of the Canadian government to place every facility necessary and available at their disposal in order that they may do that job fairly and impartially.
If the economy of our country and the philosophy behind it is correct; if there is nothing wrong with it; if we have nothing to fear in comparison with any other country, the national film board are telling the truth in their films. They are showing the situation
as it actually exists. I have sufficient confidence in the judgment and the intelligence of the Canadian people to believe that, regardless of anything they may see or hear with respect to the organization of this country in the future, they will do their job in their own way. I definitely deprecate the remarks made by the hon. member for York West. I consider it is an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people.

I suggested last year and the year before and I would suggest again that the film board should take pictures of perhaps the most beautiful scenery in Canada, Kakabeka falls with a 90-foot head, lough Lomond, Mirady park and mount McKay, which would show well all over Canada. It would not only advertise the head of the lakes but all of Canada.
Would you have the hon. member's picture with it?

I have thought it my business to go down on Tuesday and Thursday nights to see some of the pictures. They were fine pictures. I have read reviews in the United States papers about different pictures and they offer high praise for the films put out by the national film board. However, I am surprised when I find people attacking a picture about the Soviet Union, an ally that is doing so much fighting, an ally for whom we have a lot of admiration, but an ally for whom some people have nothing but a good word now and then, and no more. They will not let the people find out anything about that country. A continuation of this policy will lead to catastrophe. We should fight it every time we see any signs of it coming back to life.
I visited the Soviet Union in 1930 and I was in Stalingrad when the great tractor plant there first started producing. Lately I saw a film which showed that there was nothing left of the Stalingrad plant. The people of Russia have paid with their plant and with their blood. When I came back to this country in December, 1930, and told people what I had seen they said, "You have been looking through rose-coloured glasses; you saw what you wanted to see." A few weeks after that the Bennett government put on an embargo against products from the Soviet Union. This was sheer stupidity because we were importing very few commodities from the Soviet Union. Canada produces about ninety per cent of the world's asbestos, and shortly after that time I visited the asbestos producing area and was told by the people there that this action had been taken because

Russia was dumping asbestos in Canada. This was because of the lies spread about that country. To-day some people still try to slander the soviet people. This sort of action comes from the hon. members to my right. It appears that the spirit of Bennett is prevalent in their ranks.

I was not in the house when the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) was speaking, but apparently he referred to certain films which have been shown lately and which depict life in the Soviet Union during these war days. I have no objection to seeing a good show or a good war picture, whether it shows activities in Russia, Italy, North Africa or any other country. In motion pictures we have a most powerful medium of propaganda and I think we should try to arrive at a proper balance in the pictures shown. Recently I saw a picture; I believe its title was "Russia at War", and I must confess that I was tremendously impressed with the fortitude of the Russian people. It was a most powerful picture, and it was powerful propaganda. All pictures of that type are propaganda, whether they are meant to be or not.
As I saw that picture I asked myself, how many pictures showing Canada's war effort or pictures showing the war efforts of Great Britain and the United States are being shown in the theatres of the Soviet Union? We have produced some good pictures of our own war effort. Not many months ago a picture was shown entitled "London Can Take It", showing London after the terrible bombardment of the blitz. Pictures of that kind should be shown in other countries, including the Soviet Union.
I ask the minister, how many pictures produced in Canada-I do not confine my question to the "Canada Carries On" series, although that should be included-have been exported to be shown in other countries, and in what countries have they been shown? If the minister cannot give the information tonight, perhaps he will furnish it at some other time.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am sorry I cannot tell the hon. member for Macleod the number of Canadian pictures that have been exported. Many have been exported, especially to the United States. Canadian pictures go to the British isles and to the British dominions. Our trade commissioners and diplomatic corps see to the distribution of Canadian pictures. There have been some inquiries about, if not orders for, Canadian pictures for Russia. I regret I have not the figures this evening, but if they are required I shall be glad to make them known later on.
[Mr Hose.]

A moment ago I said that motion pictures constituted a most powerful medium of propaganda. What I am going to say now is not said in any sense of harsh criticism of the government. At the present time the government is in a rather preferred position with respect to propaganda. Any picture that portrays Canadian war industry has a psychological effect upon the people. They are inclined to think what a good government they have.
They would not take on a big task like that, would they?
I do not mean this as harsh criticism because I suppose it is quite natural. I imagine any government in power would make use of such a department to propagandize its own work.
They would not do that.

I would not say that. For instance, we see a picture of a factory going at full blast; perhaps the factory is just being officially opened, and on the screen we see the smiling countenance of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) who makes a speech into the microphone. Whether we like it or not, there is a psychological reaction in favour of the present government. Of course, it would depend upon whose face is shown on the screen, because it could work the other way. I would suggest that in any pictures which the national film board may take in future of the various political groups in Canada, it be fair to all groups. I could illustrate what I mean, but I shall not take the time to do so now.
I think we are all interested in our Canadian institutions, and one of our Canadian institutions is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I visited Toronto a few weeks ago and met some of the officials, the men who are in harness operating the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's programmes. I must confess that the C.B.C. was sold to me, and I determined that I was going out to try to sell the C.B.C. to the country, provided that it does not make any mistakes to cause me to do the very opposite. I suggest that the national film board could do something to put over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Canada. A film showing some of the equipment used, for instance, or the way in which electrical equipment is worked would be interesting. That is one way in which they could be of service to the Canadian people.

If they could get a picture of the general manager, that would help, too.

436. Post offices, including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices-further amount required, $676,000.

Sometimes we criticize
the ministers, but occasionally we have an opportunity to say something in their favour. A few days ago on the train to Toronto I sat behind two gentlemen who were praising the Postmaster General very highly. I asked one
Supply-Post Office

of them if he knew the Postmaster General. He said: "Yes; I am a postmaster myself"; and the gentleman sitting beside him said the same thing. I said, "How do. you find the Postmaster General?" "Well," he said, "he has been a great help to us." I made up my mind that on the first occasion I would bring that tribute publicly to the Postmaster General. In doing so, I hope he will not compare me with a Greek bearing gifts if I ask a favour for the Toronto "posties." The minister knows well the situation in Toronto, and he will agree that there is no part of the public service which does a better and more onerous job, and whose members are more faithful, than the postmen not only of Toronto, but of all the great cities. The burdens they carry are terrific, particularly around Christmas time. I have attended a number of their meetings and heard them tell of their remuneration, which is so small that I could hardly believe it. All I have to ask the minister, and that as a favour not to myself but to a large body of faithful government employees who richly deserve much more than they get, is that between now and the bringing down of the main estimates he carefully look into and review the remuneration paid to the " posties," and if he concurs in what I have said, that he bring in supplementary estimates, if sufficient is not provided in the main estimates, to give fitting and fair remuneration to the postal service of Canada.

I brought this matter to the attention of the house on February 3. The wages paid to postmen are out of line with those received by all other public servants in our city, particularly firemen and policemen. This question has been brought to the attention of the minister for several years, but nothing has been done about it. The whole range of salaries of the postal service in Toronto is long overdue for overhaul and a change. These fellows are doing a wonderful job, especially in war time. I agree with the hon. member for Davenport that something should be done; I know he has brought this subject to the attention of the minister before now. It has always been a surprise to me that we have not been able to get some action in this matter. -

I find myself somewhat at a loss to understand why, in an old-established department, a supplementary vote should be as large as $676,000. Would the minister care to explain it? When I turn to page 7 of the further supplementary estimates for an explanation, I find, "cost of living bonus and other pay-list items, $211,000," which is a brief

May I deal first with the question of the hon. member who last spoke? That $676,000 is divided into three items. The first one, $115,000, is for salary expenditure exclusive of increases granted under the provisions of order in council dated November 17, 1943. It is expected to be in the neighbourhood of $15,640,000, whereas the vote is only $15,524,995, leaving a shortage of $115,000. The shortage cannot be adjusted by transfers from a vote on the estimates of one branch to that of another. The second item is $350,000. This is required to pay increases granted to permanent and temporary employees under the provisions of order in council P.C. 194-8855, dated November 17, 1943. This takes care of 2,089 employees, of whom 630 are permanent and 1,459 are temporary. The third item is $211,000. This is for the cost of living bonus. The The shortage in the ordinary expenditure is estimated at $188,000, owing to the fact that treasury board directed that provision in the 1943-44 main estimates be restricted to the amount payable on September 30, 1942; therefore no provision could be made for the larger staff which we thought would be needed. When I look at this amount of $676,000, and then at the detail on page 7, I am somewhat surprised that the minister did not see to it that greater detail was given on this page. The item states, "including salaries and other expenses of headquarters and staff post offices and supplies and equipment for revenue post offices," but in the detail nothing is stated about supplies to these revenue post offices, and the item of $465,000 is stated to be for "temporary assistance". Surely a department such as the minister presides over should not have to carry

The minister complains that he should not be asked about increased compensation to rural mail carriers because it is not in this item. It is the privilege of the opposition, to inquire why not, why provision is not made for some increases for rural mail carriers. There is not a class of people in the public service of this country who are more poorly paid than the rural mail carriers. Our page boys get more money than the rural mail carriers and it is
an everlasting disgrace to the country and to the department. I know at once what the answer is, that they are not employees but contractors. That may be good enough in normal times, but with the cost of operation going as high as it is in this war, some consideration must be given to the plight of some of these people who are being held strictly to a contract. I believe that in some cases that has happened, and I suggest to the minister that the whole policy should be reviewed for the period of the war.
I am sure there is not, within the sound of my voice, a member representing a rural constituency who does not agree with the principle for which I am pleading to-night, that these people who took their contracts pre-war at low prices, in competition if you will, and who are now bound by the terms of a legal contract, should have the right to a reinvestigation and renegotiation of their contracts in the light of what they are asked to do.
I do not believe there is an employee in this house who receives a lower rate of compensation than the rural mail carriers, and it does not reflect very much credit on us, and certainly not on the department.
While I am on my feet there is another matter to which I would refer. A few weeks ago I made an inquiry of the Postmaster General with reference to the plight of certain railway mail clerks in my own province who, on what they considered the best of advice, did not elect to take advantage of the offer held out by the government twenty years ago to come in under the new scheme of the Superannuation Act, and who to-day find themselves in a precarious position with respect to their retiring allowances or whatever comes to them when they go out of office, because of reduction in the rate of interest allowed.
I am not going to go into into any further details. The minister is quite familiar with the matter, and the assistant deputy minister was good enough to explain to me the legal aspects and the effect on the men, At that time the Postmaster General indicated that it was a matter of policy for the Department of Finance. I suggest to him that he has some responsibility in trying to convince his colleague of the justice of the claim' of these men. I could put the whole matter on Hansard in detail, but I am not going to do so. The minister knows the problem to which I refer and I bespeak from him, not generosity but justice for these men, who after all are really only a small group and whose request would not represent a great charge on the public revenue. I ask for justice for them and I ask for justice for the rural mail carriers of Canada.

It might be in some, but in some of the more difficult contracts it would not, where men with competitive tenders went very low in certain cases. I am
obliged to the Chairman for his forbearance.
I merely wanted to discuss the exact point raised by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Chairman. Do I interpret your ruling to mean that I am not entitled to pursue that subject farther?

I put it to the committee if I am not as much entitled to speak on this matter as were hon. gentlemen who preceded me. I think some hon. gentlemen to my left do not thoroughly grasp the situation, nor do I think the minister was quite as frank as he might have been in describing it. Most of us will remember that last session the minister announced, much to our gratification, that certain orders in council had been passed dealing with this situation. He took credit to himself and to the government, quite naturally, for his generosity in dealing with the matter, as a result of which the lot of these men would be improved. But he was not quite so altruistic in his actions as it might appear. The real reason why increases were given-and they were given, or at least arrangements were made for some increases- was that the government found they would save money by doing so. The.cost of living, and expenses in connection with running a car, have increased so enormously that men were throwing up their contracts. Perhaps they would come to the government and say, "We cannot carry on like this", but the government would reply, "Well, we have two sureties." Often, one of them might be a parson, who would not know anything about running a rural route; but the government would add, "We will hold you to it". A great many of the rural carriers quit, and then
Supply-Post Office
the government had to put up the routes at public auction. As a result they had to pay much larger sums than they had been paying previously. Therefore they said, "We do not want to do this. If a route is put up at auction we will have to let it for four years at a high rate, so that perhaps we had better compromise". Accordingly they made inquiries and found that many of the rural carriers, who always take their contracts at less than they should, were willing to compromise. They said, "If you will give us a little extra money while the war is on, to meet the extra cost, we will not mind going back to the original lower rate at the end of the war". That seemed reasonable, and orders in council were passed providing that some official of the Post Office Department should consider the situation and, where it was found that the rural carrier was doing the work for a price at which he could not really work, with the increased cost of living, then he would be given more money for the duration of the war, with the understanding that after the war was over he would have to go back to the lower rate.
This satisfied the government, because as a result they had to pay the extra money only during the war and were not saddled with a four-year contract. It satisfied the rural carrier, because he had been willing to carry on the work at a low rate previously, and when costs went down he would be willing to continue at that low rate again. That would have been satisfactory if the arrangement had been carried out in the right spirit, but that was not done. The hon. member for York-Sunbury wanted to know how many rural mail carriers there are. I think the number is around thirteen thousand. We know that the price of a rural route is decided by public competition; the public decides what it is worth. It may be a little higher in this part of the country and a little lower in another part, but it is worth whatever the public says it is worth, at a very low estimate. It is always taken at below a reasonable price. I said to one man, "Instead of being helped, you should be ashamed for taking the contract at such a low rate". He replied, "Well, I had a Ford car and a bit of a pension, and I thought it would work out all right". He is not paid a pension in order to permit him to operate a rural mail route at less than its value.
To my mind it would have been a reasonable thing-and I spent most of last fall arguing this matter-for the government to take the prices which the public had made these routes worth. Then they would have had a guarantee that the price in future would be in proportion to what the public had said
Supply-Post Office

it should be originally, whether that price was fifteen, cents a mile in one place or twenty cents in another. Then I suggest the fair way would have been to say, "Well, we will raise all of you five or ten or whatever percentage is thought reasonable." That was not done. The matter was put into the hands of one official, probably a very fine official. I know him personally, and I am glad to say that I think he is my friend, but he had not been over all these routes. As far as my district is concerned, I have been over every rural mail route in it. This official went to work and said to one man, "You are getting fourteen cents a mile now and you want eighteen cents. Well, you will not get it; I think fourteen cents is enough." Then he would buttress his case by saying, "The man next to you is getting fourteen cents, and so is a man somewhere else," but as far as I could ascertain it was not worked out by any definite process of arithmetic. I know of one case where two rural routes ran out of one small village. One man was given an increase of seventy-two or seventy-four per cent, while the man operating the route which ran in the other direction was refused any increase at all, though his rate was lower than that of the first man. That was the sort of thing that caused all the trouble; instead of giving satisfaction it created a great deal of dissatisfaction. Most of the carriers put in for increases; those who did not get them, but saw others getting them, of course became dissatisfied. I think it would have worked all right if the government had said, "The public have beaten down the prices; this is what the public think these routes are worth, and we will give you an increase of ten per cent," or whatever increase was thought sufficient.
An hon. member to my left asked how many rural routes there were and how many carriers had been given increases. If you went into that aspect of the question you would get into a lot of trouble, because it would require an enormous amount of labour and then you would reveal percentages, which would not be very satisfactory.
If the order in council is to be believed, it was the intention of the government to relieve these men. The men would have been relieved. They would have got something to keep them going through these expensive times. The government would have been better off because, when the men threw it up, the contract had to be let at public tender; the government paid a great deal- more, and then it was let for four years, whereas now it runs for only a year and a half or until the end of the war. I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury. This is one of the items that impressed itself on my mind when I was dealing with the ordinary running expenses of the Department of Trade and Commerce. This exceptionally heavy movement was not anticipated when the estimates for the current fiscal year were submitted. The total lake shipments for the season were 344 million bushels as compared with 211 million bushels in the previous season. Increased shipments to eastern Canada were also made by rail. This increased activity is reflected in the revenue of the board, the total of which for the first nine months of the current fiscal year is 81,304,977.43, or an increase of $418,983.06 over the same period in the previous fiscal year. As to the item of 85,000 for travelling expenses, war conditions have necessitated the temporary transfer of employees for longer periods on account of changes in the routing of the grain. Congestion in storage
necessitates more supervision, and audits of stocks in eastern elevators have necessitated increased travelling expenses for this year.

The minister emphasizes the increase for temporary assistance. I cannot see the force of his argument, because there have been many years in which the movement of grain has been practically as heavy as this last year. It is based on the amount of the crop harvested, and large stocks of coarse grains were marketed this year. I would not think there would be very much more work involved than usual. Since there will not be another opportunity until after the Easter recess, I would ask the minister to make a statement now with respect to the auditing of accounts. The minister has promised a statement with respect to that, and this might be a good time to give it.
I also asked one or two other questions which I was not allowed to put on the orders of the day because they were declared out of order, and they were not allowed to go on the order paper. Perhaps the minister would make a statement now.
I did not anticipate being asked about the auditors on this item and have not that information before me, but I will get it and give it to my hon. friend later.
That is an interesting statement from the minister who is carrying on a department, that he does not know who the auditors are.

Thousands and thousands of farmers in the west and ini other parts of Canada are producing grain, and I suggest that the information given here is meagre when we take into consideration that the returns from our labours are practically decided by men in the employ of this department. Does the inspection )f quota books come under this item?
No.

Then we can let that go for the time being. The item of $75,000 for temporary assistance seems large. There is a considerable amount of grain to handle at all seasons of the year. Do those who are giving temporary assistance receive the cost of living bonus?

The hon. member will have an opportunity to get information on a number of points he has raised, some of which have to do with the operations of the Canadian wheat board and some with the board of grain commissioners, when the main estimates of the department are up for consideration. estimates for this year were being prepared. As the hon. member knows, there were some difficult problems to deal with in handling the western grain crop this year, and the expenses were considerably higher than it was anticipated. This item is to take care of unforeseen expenses.
Are the temporary employees given the cost of living bonus?

The
new employees.
There is an item for $5,000 for travelling expenses. How is that amount made up? What is the scale of travelling expenses?

How much do you allow them, for instance, for car expenses per mile?

This in-eludes, I think, inspectors carrying on registrations and so on. I imagine it has to do with inspectors travelling from one place to the other, and they would be allowed so much per mile if they owned their own ears, or be subject to some other arrangement if they did not.

Does the department provide government cars for these inspectors? I know that was a vexed question ten years ago. Every man wanted to have his own car and be paid for it. Does the department encourage employees to use their own cars; does the government provide cars; does it hire cars, or what does it do?

Speaking from memory, I think cars are handled in different ways, but the policy of the department has been to encourage a man to own his own car, the department to pay

him a per mile rate. I shall, however, be glad to take note of the hon. member's question and give him full information later.

The
minister is not able to state to-day the rate per mile?
Not at the moment.

If the
minister has not the information here I am not going to press the question.

There is a board of grain commissioners, with an assistant board of grain commissioners in each of the western provinces. I imagine these travelling expenses are the expenses of these grain commissioners and assistant grain commissioners in the course of their duty in the different parts of the country. A lot of it would be railway fares. I am inclined to think a larger proportion is represented by railway fares than by the cost of driving cars.

And hiring

DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT Marine service-
US. Marine service steamers, including icebreakers-maintenance, operation and repair- further amount required, $24,000.
Will the minister state how many icebreakers the government owns, operates and maintains and where they are operated?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
speechtext: There are five icebreakers. All operate in the gulf of St. Lawrence, and the Atlantic [DOT]-Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and some other points in the Atlantic, during the war.
What icebreaker is operating on the New Brunswick coast this year?

Of course, there was the car ferry from the mainland. Then for a while, early in the winter, there was the old Lady Grey and the Saurel between New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Cape Breton.

During a recent period there has been a great deal of interruption of the car ferry service between the mainland and the island, but no icebreaker was available. Yet I am told that we have five in operation, and certainly those
out of Sorel could not have beeen operating very much. Why was there a lack of foresight in not having an icebreaker available to keep the Northumberland strait clear, having regard to the-shall I say-ineffectiveness of the old car ferry to maintain the service? The state of communications between the mainland and Prince Edward Island is little better than a scandal, having regard to the obligation of Canada to the island. I know the difficulties very well, and I am going to refer to them a little later, when another item is up, but at the moment I want to confine my questioning of the minister to the failure of his department to provide an icebreaker as an all-time supplement to the Prince Edward Island car ferry. During the months of January, February and March not a single icebreaker has been available for that service; yet there was an icebreaker at Quebec, where she must have been doing nothing or next to nothing. The only sendee I have heard of that is being performed is the rescue of the lives of the three Quebec Airways men, which of course was most commendable, and from that point of view it was very fortunate that she was available. But we have at least two big icebreakers with headquarters in the lower St. Lawrence or in the vicinity of Quebec, and after navigation closes they cannot have anything to do for months. My complaint against the minister's department is that one of these icebreakers should have been kept available in the Northumberland strait to take care of the greatly increased heavy traffic or to keep open the channels for the greatly increased heavy traffic which has developed. Unless relief comes very soon there will be an enormous loss to the shippers of Prince Edward Island, and there will be great difficulty in obtaining transit of the large numbers of cars of fertilizer which have arrived at Tormentine for transmission across the strait. I think the service has not been good enough, and I suggest that it could have been greatly improved if the minister had had foresight enough to have had in Northumberland strait during this season one of those big icebreakers which have probably been tied up at the wharf at Quebec or Sorel for the last several weeks.
Evidently the hon. member is misinformed, because there is no icebreaker at Sorel.
Well,where are they?

There is an icebreaker called the Saurel which was and is almost always in the winter time in the gulf of St Lawrence.
Supply-Transport
I misunderstood the minister. Where was she.

She was working between Halifax, Sydney and Newfoundland, and she left Newfoundland to come to the rescue of the three men who were saved last week in the gulf of St. Lawrence. There are no icebreakers tied up at any wharf, whether at Quebec or at any other place, during the winter.

Was she breaking ice in Halifax harbour, or outside
Halifax, or between Halifax and Sydney?

Between Halifax, Canso, Sydney and Newfoundland, and late in the fall, between Prince Edward Island, Pictou and the Magdalen islands. But during the months of January and February that icebreaker was detailed to do some special work in the gulf of St. Lawrence towards Newfoundland.

That is
one out of five. Where are the rest of them?

Two were employed as
usual, breaking a channel from Quebec to Montreal.

In the
winter time?
In the winter time. That has been done for years, and it is a necessity.
I have no doubt it has been done for years, but why the necessity? There is no winter shipping into Montreal.

Oh, no, but there would be floods in the spring all along the banks of the St. Lawrence, and especially around the island of Montreal, if that work were not done in the winter time.
The other icebreaker was recalled from Cape Breton to help in certain war work in the gulf of St. Lawrence. My hon. friend says that there was negligence or lack of foresight on the part of the department in not bringing a powerful icebreaker to the rescue of the Prince Edward Island. I must inform him that early in the winter, when the Prince Edward Island began to have difficulties in crossing, suggestions were made to the engineers and officials of the department to bring an icebreaker to break the channel to help her. I was informed by officers of the department in whom I have full confidence that the Prince Edward Island was just as powerful an icebreaker as there was in the government service, and, second, that the bringing of another one into that area would be simply a nuisance to her and would not help a bit in clearing the channel. For that reason, no other icebreaker

was taken into that area, and this was confirmed, I am told, by the captain of the Prince Edward Island, who did not want to be bothered by having another icebreaker in his way.
I agree that this has been a very severe winter, owing to ice conditions and adverse winds, which kept the channel practically full of ice, so that on many days the service was interrupted. There were very few days on which there were no crossings; on many days there were a few crossings, and it took all the power of the boat to wade her way through the ice, so that hardly any load of freight could be taken off.
This is a situation over which we have no control. Every consideration was given to cope with it, and officers of the department, who have been in the service for many years, engineers, marine agents, ship captains, were all consulted and all gave the same opinion.
The situation with regard to the ferry between New Brunswick on the mainland and the island since last Saturday up to yesterday had fortunately improved greatly, and on three days during this week the ferry took an average of 100 cars each way every day.

Well,
spring is here.

But it was not spring there yesterday, unfortunately, if the hon. member wants to know. However, I hope that next week the situation will have cleared sufficiently to enable the car ferry to take its full quota of freight cars on each trip and carry on its average of from ten to fourteen trips a day, thus relieving the congestion of traffic on either side of the channel.

My information last week, when I raised the question on the orders of the day, was that there were between 500 and
1,000	cars of farm products, to a large extent potatoes for seed for other parts of Canada. Could the minister indicate that the present position is in regard to the congestion? How many cars are waiting at Borden for shipment to Tormentine and vice versa?
My hon. friend is slightly off in his estimate of the cars that were waiting for shipment to either side.
I believe it was Premier Jones of Prince Edward Island who gave the figures, though I am not sure.

On one day about two weeks ago there were 565 cars awaiting shipment to the island from the mainland, but they were cars of material which had not first or second priority for transshipment. During the winter, provisions and coal got

Supply-Transport
first priority to the island, and coming this way, potatoes and agricultural products of all kinds had priority.
I have the record for practically every day of the last two months. Of course, there may be 6,000 or 7,000 cars of goods on the island, not loaded. There might be a quantity sufficient to make up 6,000 or 7,000 cars; but as far as the records show, on March 27, three days ago, there were awaiting shipment at Borden six cars and no empties, and at Tor-mentine there were 182 loads ready to be taken over. At one time two weeks ago there were 565 carloads of goods waiting for shipment to the island, and that number was reduced to 182

That would be natural. If such a large number of cars were waiting to go over to the island, there would not be such a large number waiting on the island because they could not have crossed to get their load.

But the record shows that for days prior to the 27th the Canadian National Railways carried over empty cars which enabled them to cross over many more times than had the cars been full of merchandise, because the load was less on the boat, and this helped the farmers of the island to move their goods. For the last ten days the average of empty cars taken over was fifty a day, but for three days there were 100 cars each day taken over and for three days 100 cars each day taken back. I admit that if there had been more cars over and greater facilities, if all the cars which are loaded for transshipment had been taken over before the 27th, it would have greatly relieved the situation on the island.

Whoever is responsible, I think it is generally recognized by those of us who do not come from that part of Canada, that the situation is at best terrible so far as the island is concerned. Anyone who goes there recognizes at once that the place is insular not only from the point of view of geography but from the point of view of confederation itself, and something will have to be done pretty soon, having in mind what the premier himself says. When the premier of a province starts talking about damages which that island could claim against confederated Canada the situation must be pretty serious, and I think the minister must have been well apprised of that.
I have been apprised of the situation.

I am sorry I have not with me at the moment the language used by Premier Jones of Prince Edward Island. Everything I have said relative to this service would be trite in comparison with what he has said about it, and I have no doubt the minister fully understands his language. The trouble, however, is that they did not do very much about it; they waited for nature to take care of the situation. What the minister told me about the icebreaker was just that he allowed his own judgment and that of his officials to be overruled by the master of the Prince Edward Island and the other engineer. The minister's own instincts were good, but he did not follow them up. They never tried the experiment of having the Saurel or some other icebreaker in there. That is the fault I find with the minister. They allowed the condition to remain and did not even experiment in trying to break up this ice in the winter months. Therefore I think the minister is reprehensible for not having tried to carry out his own suggestion. I suggest that the Prince Edward Island is an old ship. How many times has she broken down this winter? How many days' delay has been due to break-downs in the mechanism of the ship herself? If the minister has the record with him I think it will show that a good many trips were lost because of break-downs in the mechanism of this old ferry which is now in use.
I do not know what the war necessities are of which the minister speaks in connection with the use of bigger icebreakers out in the St. Lawrence, and possibly it is not proper that he should tell us, though I cannot conceive why. I do not think there are any enemy submarines in the St. Lawrence in midwinter. Of course, if merchandise has to be taken to Newfoundland, as I assume is the case, an icebreaker is necessary to keep open the lines of transportation. But I suggest that the people of Prince Edward Island are equally concerned about their communications and their right to uninterrupted traffic. I know that no fighting is going on in Newfoundland; I know we have a number of draftees there; I know there are United States armed services in Newfoundland, and I suppose the Canadian government has some obligation to them, though I do not know just what it may be. I suggest to the minister that he has failed in his duty in not making an attempt that he himself thought was the right thing to do. Therefore I say he deserves the censure of this committee.

Nevertheless I submit that I did not fail. If my views were not carried out it was because of the advice and counsel

Supply-Transport

of experienced men in charge not only of the icebreakers but of the ferry as well. I could not prevail upon men with years of experience in winter navigation on the St. Lawrence to do things which, in their very best judgment, they would not want to do. I made a suggestion which as a layman I thought was feasible and practical, but I was told by men who were supposed to know better that it was not practical, and I accepted their views.

I have had many communications this year and in previous years with respect to the inadequacy of the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The people of the maritime provinces are not satisfied; certainly the people of Prince Edward Island have no reason to be satisfied with what has been done to serve their necessities during the last two years. The general opinion, which is widely supported, is that steps should have been taken to meet the situation immediately after the Charlottetown was lost. I believe that ship was lost through gross carelessness, while the person responsible for the loss was bonused or subsidized or pensioned off as a result. Steps to ensure a steady supply of beef for the meat trade have been completed by the wartime prices and trade board, which has also finalized regulations for year-round pricing.
Last October the board stated that wholesale ceiling prices for beef reached on'May 27 would remain in force for an indefinite period. At any time in the coming year when the market is not well supplied, retailers will be protected by these wholesale ceilings.
Wholesalers and producers also are protected. Floor prices have been set on dressed beef which next fall and winter will correspond to the seasonal ceiling prices of last fall and winter. The Department of Agriculture will prevent beef prices from falling below these levels by buying dressed beef whenever a surplus supply appears to endanger the market. Otherwise the market will be permitted to take its normal course.
From these purchases the department will build reserves. The reserves will be used in periods of scarcity to meet requirements of meat dealers under rationing. What is left will be used for possible Allied needs.
From May 27 to August 14 the floor price for carcass beef will be one-quarter cent per pound less than the wholesale prices set in order 252. From August 16 to September 18 the floor price will be one cent below the ceiling and from September 29 to December 18 it will be at the level of last year's ceiling for the same period, that is, two and one-quarter cents below this year's ceiling. On December 20 the floor price will be raised by one-half cent per pound. Further one-half cent increases will take effect February 7. March 20 and April 24. On April 24, 1944, the floor price will be back to one-quarter cent below the ceiling.

The price of beef wholesale cannot go above the ceiling price fixed. That naturally governs the retail price, and in that way the consumers are protected. When the wholesale price of beef declines according to the terms of these orders, the element of competition comes in and the sale price of beef in the butcher shops falls owing to the operation of ordinary competition. I believe it is correct, although I have not verified it, that the prices are checked through steps taken by the wartime prices and trade board.
